title: You, sir — choosing the right "you"
goal: Navigate the one genuinely difficult thing about beginner Indonesian: there is no neutral word for "you". Learn who gets *Bapak*, who gets *Mas*, when *kamu* is warm and when it is rude — and pick up possession on the way.
bekal: address a stranger, a colleague, a waiter and a friend, each correctly
say my, your, his and her by putting the owner **after** the thing

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hari pertama di kantor

notes: **The pronoun problem is real, and it is the only hard thing on this page.** English "you" is a single safe word. In Indonesian you must choose, and the choice announces the relationship. The good news: getting it slightly too polite is invisible, while getting it too familiar is not. When in doubt, be too polite.

**Bapak / Ibu are the everyday solution.** They literally mean "father" and "mother", and Indonesians use them for any adult they should be respectful to — a boss, an official, a stranger, an older shopkeeper. They work both as "you" (*Bapak dari mana?* = "where are you from, sir?") and as a title before a name (*Pak Hendra*). Shortened, they are *Pak* and *Bu*.

**Beliau is "he/she" with respect built in.** Rina uses it for her boss instead of *dia*. Nothing is wrong with *dia* — it is neutral for everybody — but *beliau* is a small courtesy that will be noticed if you use it about someone's teacher, parent or superior.

**Kamu is warm between equals and offensive upwards.** Rina invites Sarah to use it (*pakai kamu saja*) because they are the same age. Never open with *kamu* to a stranger, an older person or anyone in authority. The rule of thumb Indonesians themselves use: wait until the other person uses it with you.

**Mau, dong.** *Dong* is a particle with no dictionary meaning — it softens a request or adds a friendly nudge, roughly "go on then" or "please do". Indonesian is full of these little words. Unit 20 collects them; for now just recognise that *dong*, *sih*, *kok* and *deh* are tone, not content.

grammars.title: The full pronoun table
body: Learn the middle column first — it is never wrong. The right-hand column is what you will actually hear.
after: ⚠️ **Kita and kami are not interchangeable, and English cannot tell them apart.** *Kita makan* said to your guest means "we (you and I) are eating". *Kami makan* means "we are eating and you are not". Say *kami* to someone you have just invited to dinner and you have accidentally excluded them.

**Mas** (young man) and **Mbak** (young woman) are how you address waiters, drivers, shop staff and anyone roughly your own age or younger in most of Java and beyond. *Mas, permisi!* is the single most useful attention-getting phrase in the country.

💬 In Jakarta you will constantly hear *gue* (I) and *lo* (you). It is Jakarta slang, it is everywhere in social media, and it is genuinely rude in the wrong setting. Recognise it; do not use it until an Indonesian friend tells you to.

grammars.title: Possession: the owner goes last
body: There are no possessive words to learn. You take the thing, and you put the owner behind it — exactly the order that gave you *buku ini* in Unit 2.
after: The same order works for things that own things: *pintu rumah* = "door house" = the door of the house. Whatever is possessed comes first.
💬 With *aku* and *kamu* the pronoun usually shrinks and glues on: *bukuku* (my book), *bukumu* (your book). You will see these constantly in songs and messages.

sections.title: -nya, the most useful suffix in the language

blocks.text: *-nya* attaches to the end of a noun and does three different jobs. Beginners meet it in a shop on day one — *Berapa harganya?* — and then meet it everywhere else for the rest of their lives.

Which job it is doing is settled by the situation, and Indonesians never find it ambiguous. *Kopinya enak* said in a café means "the coffee here is good"; said about your friend's cup it means "his coffee is good".

Phrases with *-nya* worth memorising whole today: *Berapa harganya?* (how much is it?), *Siapa namanya?* (what's his/her name?), *Bagaimana rasanya?* (how does it taste?), *Di mana tempatnya?* (where is the place?).
Indonesia has no equivalent of clicking your fingers, and raising your voice is worse than useless. This is the whole toolkit.

⚠️ Do not use *Hey!* or *You!* — both exist in English-influenced speech and both land as rude. And never beckon with your palm up and one finger, as English speakers do; Indonesians beckon with the palm **down**, fingers scooping toward themselves.

One more piece of body language worth more than a paragraph of grammar: when you hand something to someone, or receive it, use your **right hand**. The left hand alone is impolite across most of Indonesia.
